items.title: Elasmotherium at Dawn
items.caption: Late Pleistocene steppe: Elasmotherium, the giant 'Siberian unicorn' rhino, stands in frost-covered grass at sunrise, its breath steaming in the cold air. Accuracy note: the AI placed the horn toward the snout, whereas Elasmotherium's horn sat on its forehead.
items.credit: AI-generated image (Grok Imagine). Artistic reconstruction, not a photograph.

items.title: Last Mammoths of Wrangel Island
items.caption: Wrangel Island, about 4,000 years ago: a small herd of woolly mammoths, among the last of their kind, wades through cotton-grass tundra under the midnight sun beside the Chukchi Sea.
items.credit: AI-generated image (Grok Imagine). Artistic reconstruction, not a photograph.

items.title: Sabre-Tooth Above the Tar Seeps
items.caption: Late Pleistocene Rancho La Brea, about 20,000 years ago: a Smilodon fatalis rests on a sunlit rock above the glossy tar seeps of what is now Los Angeles, with oak and cypress woodland behind.
items.credit: AI-generated image (Grok Imagine). Artistic reconstruction, not a photograph.

items.title: Irish Elk in the Morning Mist
items.caption: Late-glacial Ireland, about 13,000 years ago: a Megaloceros giganteus stag, the giant 'Irish elk', stands in a misty lakeside meadow of sedges and birch scrub in early autumn light. Accuracy note: the AI drew tall, narrow antlers; a real Irish elk's antlers spread very wide with broad flat palms, up to about 3.6 m across.
items.credit: AI-generated image (Grok Imagine). Artistic reconstruction, not a photograph.

items.title: Ichthyosaurs Among the Ammonites
items.caption: Late Jurassic seas, about 160 million years ago: a pod of big-eyed Ophthalmosaurus ichthyosaurs hunts through a swirling school of ammonites in sunlit blue water. Accuracy note: the AI gave these Ophthalmosaurus rows of prominent teeth; the real animal had small, reduced teeth suited to soft prey like squid.
items.credit: AI-generated image (Grok Imagine). Artistic reconstruction, not a photograph.

items.title: Arthropleura in the Coal Swamp
items.caption: Late Carboniferous coal-swamp forest, about 305 million years ago (Euramerica): a two-metre Arthropleura crawls over moss beneath Lepidodendron scale trees while a Meganeura griffinfly patrols overhead. Accuracy note: the body is rendered more domed than the flattened real animal, and the griffinfly looks smaller than its true 70 cm wingspan.
items.credit: AI-generated image (Grok Imagine). Artistic reconstruction, not a photograph.

items.title: Pteranodon Colony on the Chalk Cliffs
items.caption: Late Cretaceous Kansas, Western Interior Seaway, about 85 million years ago: a Pteranodon longiceps nesting colony on chalky sea cliffs. Accuracy note: some animals have overly long, bird-like necks and a few flyers look tailed and bird-like; Pteranodon eggs were probably soft-shelled and buried, not left exposed in the open.
items.credit: AI-generated image (Grok Imagine). Artistic reconstruction, not a photograph.

items.title: Glyptodons on the Pleistocene Pampas
items.caption: Late Pleistocene Argentine Pampas (~20,000 years ago): a pair of car-sized Glyptodon, armored relatives of armadillos, grazing at golden hour, with camelids and a lone Macrauchenia in the distance. Accuracy note: The shells show some armadillo-style banding, but a real Glyptodon carapace was one rigid dome of fused hexagonal plates. The tails are smoother than the real ringed, armored tails, and the distant Macrauchenia looks llama-like, without its trunk-like snout.
items.credit: AI-generated image (Grok Imagine). Artistic reconstruction, not a photograph.

items.title: Coelacanths at the Reef Cave
items.caption: Two West Indian Ocean coelacanths (Latimeria chalumnae) at the mouth of a deep volcanic reef cave off the Comoros, about 200 meters down, in the present day. This lineage dates back about 400 million years and was thought to be extinct until 1938. Accuracy note: the AI made the white blotches denser and more mottled than the sparse spots on real coelacanths, and some fins look more ray-like than the real thick, fleshy lobes.
items.credit: AI-generated image (Grok Imagine). Artistic reconstruction, not a photograph.

items.title: Paraceratherium at the Woodland Edge
items.caption: A herd of Paraceratherium, giant hornless rhinoceroses and among the largest land mammals ever, browses tall trees at the edge of an open woodland in Central Asia about 30 million years ago, during the Oligocene. Accuracy note: the AI gave the animals overly long, giraffe-like necks held nearly upright, while the real neck was shorter and thicker under a heavier head. The flat-topped trees also look more like modern African acacia savanna than Oligocene Asian woodland.
items.credit: AI-generated image (Grok Imagine). Artistic reconstruction, not a photograph.

items.title: Spinosaurus in the Kem Kem River
items.caption: Spinosaurus aegyptiacus seizes a large Mawsonia, a coelacanth relative, while wading a muddy river in the Kem Kem system of North Africa, about 95 million years ago in the mid-Cretaceous. Accuracy note: the AI drew the sail as a rounded fan, but the real Spinosaurus sail was taller toward the middle of the back and more rectangular. The tail also lacks the tall, paddle-like fin that fossils show, and the snout is shorter and blunter than the real long, narrow one.
items.credit: AI-generated image (Grok Imagine). Artistic reconstruction, not a photograph.

items.title: Dimetrodon at Dawn on the Permian Floodplain
items.caption: Dimetrodon, a sail-backed synapsid (closer to mammals than to dinosaurs), basks on a red mudbank of an Early Permian river floodplain in what is now north Texas, about 285 million years ago, while a second animal warms up across the channel. Accuracy note: the AI gave the sail a fan-like, frilled outline; the real sail was a skin membrane over separate long spines, with a more even curve. The head is too low and crocodile-like, missing Dimetrodon's tall, deep skull and big front teeth, and the palm-like trees look more modern than Permian seed ferns and conifers.
items.credit: AI-generated image (Grok Imagine). Artistic reconstruction, not a photograph.

items.title: Cave Bears at the Den Mouth
items.caption: A cave bear (Ursus spelaeus) and her cub stand at the mouth of a limestone den above an alpine valley in Late Pleistocene Europe, about 40,000 years ago. Claw scratches mark the walls and old bones litter the floor, much like the real bear caves of the Alps. Accuracy note: the AI drew modern brown bears. Real cave bears were bulkier, with a high domed forehead, a steep brow and a shorter, broader face, and they ate mostly plants.
items.credit: AI-generated image (Grok Imagine). Artistic reconstruction, not a photograph.

items.title: Deinotherium on the Miocene Riverbank
items.caption: A Deinotherium and her calf browse along a hazy forested river in Late Miocene Europe, about 9 million years ago. This giant elephant relative was among the largest land mammals of its time and stripped leaves from trees with its unusual tusks. Accuracy note: the AI drew a modern elephant with tusks coming from the upper jaw. Deinotherium had no upper tusks, only two that curved down and back from the lower jaw, with a shorter trunk, longer legs and smaller ears.
items.credit: AI-generated image (Grok Imagine). Artistic reconstruction, not a photograph.

items.title: Woolly Mammoths on the Autumn Steppe
items.caption: A herd of woolly mammoths (Mammuthus primigenius) with a calf crosses frost-dusted grassland on the mammoth steppe of Beringia, the Late Pleistocene land bridge between Siberia and Alaska, about 30,000 years ago. Accuracy note: the anatomy is largely right, with the high domed head, sloping back, small ears and spiraling tusks; the coats are drawn a uniform ginger, while frozen carcasses suggest mammoth hair varied from dark brown to lighter shades.
items.credit: AI-generated image (Grok Imagine). Artistic reconstruction, not a photograph.

items.title: Griffinfly Over the Carboniferous Coal Swamp
items.caption: A giant griffinfly, Meganeura, hovers over a misty Late Carboniferous coal swamp about 305 million years ago, while the two-meter millipede Arthropleura crawls along a mossy log beneath Lepidodendron scale trees and Calamites horsetails in what is now Europe. Accuracy note: the diamond-patterned scale-tree bark and horsetails are well rendered, but the millipede is drawn more like a giant pill bug and the tree ferns look a little like modern palms.
items.credit: AI-generated image (Grok Imagine). Artistic reconstruction, not a photograph.

items.title: Haast's Eagle and Moa in the Beech Forest
items.caption: A Haast's eagle, Hieraaetus moorei, the largest eagle known, swoops on a South Island giant moa in a misty southern beech forest in New Zealand about 1,000 years ago, before both went extinct after people arrived. Accuracy note: the shaggy, wingless moa and the eagle's huge talons are well drawn, but the eagle looks too big next to the moa, which really stood up to about 2 meters tall at the back, and the eagle's plumage looks like a modern golden eagle's.
items.credit: AI-generated image (Grok Imagine). Artistic reconstruction, not a photograph.

items.title: Sabertooths at the La Brea Tar Seep
items.caption: A pair of Smilodon fatalis stalk a Bison antiquus mired in an asphalt seep at Rancho La Brea, in the Los Angeles basin about 30,000 years ago, while dire wolves watch from the grass. Accuracy note: trapped herbivores really did draw predators into the tar, but Imagine gave the cats long tails and short, hidden sabers, and the shaggy bison looks closer to a modern buffalo.
items.credit: AI-generated image (Grok Imagine). Artistic reconstruction, not a photograph.

items.title: Dunkleosteus Over the Devonian Reef
items.caption: The armored placoderm Dunkleosteus terrelli cruises over a reef of corals and crinoids in a Late Devonian sea about 370 million years ago, as small fish and coiled ammonoids scatter. Accuracy note: the sharp bony jaw blades, which the real animal had instead of teeth, are roughly right, but Imagine drew the body scaly and grouper-like, while the real animal was armored at the front and its rear body plan is largely unknown, probably more shark-like.
items.credit: AI-generated image (Grok Imagine). Artistic reconstruction, not a photograph.

items.title: Giant Ground Sloth on the Pampas
items.caption: A Megatherium americanum rears up to strip leaves from a lone tree on the Argentine pampas about 15,000 years ago, while a second sloth and an armored glyptodont graze in the golden grass. Accuracy note: rearing on hind legs and tail to browse matches the fossil evidence, but Imagine drew the sloth far too small (Megatherium was elephant-sized and taller than the tree) and with a bear-like face.
items.credit: AI-generated image (Grok Imagine). Artistic reconstruction, not a photograph.

items.title: Chambered Nautiluses on the Palau Reef Wall
items.caption: Three chambered nautiluses (Nautilus pompilius) rise up a deep reef wall off Palau at dusk, as they do each night from the depths. Their lineage stretches back about 500 million years, through the heyday of their ammonite cousins. Accuracy note: the tiger-striped shells and tentacle clusters are close to life, though the shells' brown bands are drawn slightly too regular.
items.credit: AI-generated image (Grok Imagine). Artistic reconstruction, not a photograph.

items.title: Irish Elk in the Misty Bog at Dawn
items.caption: A bull Irish elk (Megaloceros giganteus) stands in a fog-wrapped Ice Age bog at autumn dawn while two hinds graze behind him. The giant deer roamed Europe and Asia until about 7,700 years ago, and its antlers could span 3.6 meters, the largest of any deer known. Accuracy note: the coat, shoulder hump and habitat are plausible, but the antlers have too many spiky tines and not enough of the broad, flat palms real Megaloceros carried, and they look a bit small for this bull's size.
items.credit: AI-generated image (Grok Imagine). Artistic reconstruction, not a photograph.

items.title: Archelon in the Cretaceous Seaway
items.caption: Archelon, the largest sea turtle known, glides through sunlit water in the shallow Western Interior Seaway that split North America about 75 million years ago. Adults reached about 4 meters long, with a leathery, ridged shell and a sharply hooked beak. Accuracy note: the hooked beak and huge front flippers are right, but this turtle has a scaly, modern-looking shell and gives no sense of its true giant size. The ammonites in the background look more like small snails.
items.credit: AI-generated image (Grok Imagine). Artistic reconstruction, not a photograph.

items.title: Woolly Rhino on the Frosted Steppe
items.caption: A woolly rhinoceros (Coelodonta antiquitatis) crosses the frost-covered mammoth steppe in early winter, head held low to graze. Woolly rhinos ranged across Ice Age Europe and northern Asia until about 14,000 years ago. Accuracy note: the shaggy coat, shoulder hump and low-slung head are right, but the front horn is round and curves upward like a tusk, while real Coelodonta horns were flattened from side to side and swept forward. The second horn also sits too far back, close to the eyes.
items.credit: AI-generated image (Grok Imagine). Artistic reconstruction, not a photograph.

items.title: Thylacine in the Tasmanian Rainforest at Dusk
items.caption: A thylacine, or Tasmanian tiger (Thylacinus cynocephalus), pauses on a mossy log in a misty Tasmanian rainforest at dusk. This striped marsupial predator vanished from mainland Australia about 3,000 years ago, and the last known one died in Hobart Zoo in 1936. Unconfirmed sightings still keep alive hope that some survived. Accuracy note: the long head, stiff-legged stance and sandy coat are close, but there are too many stripes and they are too bold. They should be fewer and fade out at the hips, not run onto the tail. The tail should also be thicker at its base, and the ears a little more rounded.
items.credit: AI-generated image (Grok Imagine). Artistic reconstruction, not a photograph.

items.title: Giant Moa in the Misty Beech Forest
items.caption: South Island giant moa (Dinornis robustus). New Zealand's southern beech forests, about 600 years ago, shortly before moa were hunted to extinction after people arrived. The tallest bird that ever lived, females could stand about 3 metres with the neck raised, and moa had no wings at all, not even vestigial bones. Accuracy note: the legs here are too slender (real moa had very thick, heavy leg bones), the bill is a little long and curved compared with the short, blunt, flat-headed skull, and the bird is shown at the smaller end of the species' size range.
items.credit: AI-generated image (Grok Imagine). Artistic reconstruction, not a photograph.

items.title: Quetzalcoatlus on the Cretaceous Floodplain
items.caption: Quetzalcoatlus northropi, a giant azhdarchid pterosaur. A river floodplain in what is now west Texas, about 68 million years ago, near the very end of the Age of Dinosaurs. Standing as tall as a giraffe with a wingspan of around 10 metres, it likely spent much of its time walking on all fours, picking off small animals on the ground like a giant stork. Accuracy note: the head and beak are too small and slender for the animal's size (the real skull was enormous, well over 2 metres long), the folded wings look more like loose flaps than limbs held tight to walk on, and the distant herd looks more like small sauropods than the hadrosaurs that were meant to be there.
items.credit: AI-generated image (Grok Imagine). Artistic reconstruction, not a photograph.

items.title: Trilobites in the Ordovician Crinoid Garden
items.caption: Isotelus trilobites among stalked crinoids. A warm, shallow tropical sea over what is now eastern North America, about 450 million years ago in the Ordovician Period, long before fish ruled the oceans. Isotelus was one of the largest trilobites, sometimes over 40 cm long, and shared the sea floor with crinoids (animals related to starfish that look like flowers) and long straight-shelled cephalopods. Accuracy note: the trilobite eyes look like round, cartoonish eyeballs rather than raised crescent-shaped compound eyes, some shells are too lumpy and segmented compared with Isotelus's smooth, broad shield, and the cephalopod in the distance looks more like a squid or fish than a straight cone-shelled orthocone.
items.credit: AI-generated image (Grok Imagine). Artistic reconstruction, not a photograph.
